The key cutter at the hardware store had been listening to the same baseball game for thirty-one years.

It was the game his daughter had pitched in July of 1994. He had called it into a tape recorder from the bleachers, ostensibly for his wife, who was working a double. Over the years the recording had migrated from cassette to CD to a little blue rectangle his grandson had loaded for him. The sound had not improved in transit.

“Does she win?” I asked.

“I should hope so by now,” he said.

He was cutting me a key to my mother’s house. She had taken to locking herself out when she went to get the paper. I’d suggested a combination box, but she didn’t like the idea of her rabbits knowing the code. This was a joke. Lately I had developed the bad habit of taking a moment to decide.

On the recording, someone hit a foul ball. The key cutter’s younger voice said, “That’s coming this way,” followed by a dreadful clatter.

“Got you?” I asked.

“Lemonade.”

He ran a wire brush over the new key. I asked him if his daughter still played.

“Debbie? Lord, no. She sells industrial carpeting. That’s her on the wall.”

In the photograph a woman about my age stood beside a tremendous roll of gray carpet, giving the camera two thumbs up.

“Hospital in Akron,” he said. “Whole building.”

Then he held up a finger, and we listened. There was the ordinary hiss of wind against a microphone, a bat pinging somewhere on another diamond, the younger man saying he thought the count was two and one. Just behind his voice, a woman said, “Here, give me that. You’re missing her.”

The sound changed. The wind went away. For several seconds you could hear the hollow knock of a ball landing in a glove.

“My wife,” he said. “Got somebody to cover the end of her shift.”

“So she saw the game.”

“Most of it.”

He put both keys on the counter. I couldn’t tell which one I had come in with until I saw the little fan of brass dust beside the new one.

At my mother’s house I tried the copy. It worked if I pulled the door toward me, which was also true of the original. I found her in the kitchen with the newspaper spread open to the crossword.

“Four letters,” she said. “A kind of nut.”

“Pecan.”

“Count on your fingers, honey.”

I sat down. The kettle was beginning to make its preliminary noises. Outside, one of the rabbits was eating the parsley she had planted expressly for herself and, in actual practice, entirely for the rabbits.

“Cola,” I said.

She counted the squares with the end of her pencil. “Cola nut. Well, look at you.”

I put the spare key on the table.

“What’s that for?”

“In case you lock yourself out.”

“Not much use to me in here, is it?”

I picked it up again.

She filled in a few more answers while I made the tea. I told her about the man in the hardware store. I told her about the lemonade and the hospital carpeting and the moment the woman took the microphone. My mother listened with her pencil resting in the crease of the paper.

“Did the girl win?” she asked.

“I think so.”

“You didn’t stay to find out?”

“My key was done.”

She considered this a poor excuse. We drank our tea. After a while she got up to fetch the biscuit tin, and I noticed she wasn’t limping anymore. I couldn’t remember when she had stopped. For months I had watched that bad knee of hers every time she crossed a room, and then one day, apparently, I had quit watching.

“Oatmeal or ginger?” she asked.

“Ginger.”

“Good. The oatmeal are gone.”

I put the key on my ring, between my own front door key and the little useless one for a bicycle stolen in 2008. My mother folded the crossword back to expose the clues she hadn’t done. I could have stayed and helped, except that helping my mother with a crossword required sitting quietly until she had answered all the questions herself.

I stayed. She had twelve across wrong, but it worked itself out.
